text: The IR plan from Lesson 5 covers the general process: classify, communicate, escalate, notify. A playbook goes a level deeper. It's a specific, pre-thought-out sequence of steps for one known scenario type, written before that scenario ever happens.

The whole point of a playbook is where the thinking happens. The plan handles any incident in general. A playbook handles one known scenario in specific detail -- exact steps, decided calmly in advance by people with time to think it through, instead of improvised live, under pressure, by whoever happens to be on call that night. Most mature SOCs keep a small library of these for their most common, most damaging scenario types.

A ransomware playbook isolates affected hosts from the network without powering them off, since powering off can destroy memory-resident evidence. It identifies the ransomware family from the note or file extension to check for a known decryptor. Critically, it verifies backups are intact and isolated before anyone assumes they're usable -- the step teams skip constantly when it isn't written down. Any ransom-payment decision routes through legal, executives, and the insurer, never a solo technical call.

A business email compromise playbook resets the mailbox's credentials and MFA, audits for forwarding rules the attacker quietly added, and reviews OAuth app grants on the account. Just as important: it notifies Finance immediately, because BEC is usually financial fraud wearing a technical disguise, and a fraudulent wire transfer needs to be flagged or clawed back fast.

A data exfiltration playbook focuses on identifying what data left and how -- cloud upload, email, removable media -- and preserving DLP and proxy logs before they roll off, since legal's notification decision depends entirely on what was actually taken. An insider threat playbook adds a step the others don't need: looping in HR and Legal before any technical action, because tipping off the employee too early, or acting without proper authorization, can destroy both the evidence and the organization's legal position.

Four scenario types, four playbooks, each written in advance so nobody has to invent the response live. Next, Lesson 7 turns to the people running these playbooks -- the IR team's roles and a RACI model for who decides, who executes, and who's simply kept informed.
